screens.title: Prototyping & Iteration in Level Design
screens.subtitle: Build fast, test early, and refine by observing real players.

narration.text: In this lesson we'll ground the idea that the best levels emerge from cycles of quick builds, playtest feedback, and repeated refinement. Prototyping means making simplified, functional versions of your level using basic shapes so you can test flow, movement, and core mechanics before committing art. Iteration is the rhythm that follows: test, learn, change, and test again. Together they save time, reduce wasted art work, and reveal what actually feels fun. For example, a jump that looks reasonable on paper may feel too short when a player tries to cross it in a blockout. Prototyping exposes that problem early, when moving a cube is minutes, not weeks. We'll also see practical tools designers use, like ProBuilder or BSP brushes, and learn a simple blockout workflow you can apply immediately. Watch for common traps — over-detailing too soon, ignoring playtest data, or designing in isolation — because they turn quick experiments into expensive rework. By the end you'll know how to make a playable blockout, run a focused playtest, and iterate from real player observations. Think about one level you can block out this week and what single question you'll test first.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Prototyping makes design problems visible early; iteration turns player data into concrete improvements.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why prototyping is a core practice in level design, describe the stages of blockout construction, use basic level editor tools to create initial layouts, and run playtests that yield actionable feedback. Specifically, you will learn to evaluate flow and pacing in a greybox, judge jump distances and cover placement from player movement, and interpret playtest observations without jumping too quickly to solutions. For example, when a tester repeatedly fails a jump, you'll first check scale and approach lines in the blockout rather than adding visual hints. These objectives matter because they shift your focus from aesthetic polish to mechanical clarity early, saving time and improving the player's experience. We'll also introduce small mnemonics to remember each step during quick iterations. Practice and verified milestones will help you show competency: a playable blockout, a concise test plan, and a documented iteration after feedback. Start thinking about which skill you want to practice first: building, testing, or interpreting player data.

screens.title: What is Prototyping in Level Design?
screens.subtitle: A precise definition and practical role in development

narration.text: Prototyping in level design is the practice of creating early, simplified versions of spaces and mechanics to test ideas quickly. The point is to remove visual complexity so you can judge scale, movement, and gameplay without distraction. For example, a designer might place large cubes to represent walls and columns and use flat colors to indicate functional elements like cover or climbable platforms. This lets you answer specific questions: can the player traverse that gap, does the sightline let players see an enemy at the right moment, or does a corridor become a frustrating bottleneck? A common misconception is that prototyping replaces final design; it does not. Instead it validates or rejects high-level decisions before artists invest time. Prototyping also serves as a communication tool: other team members can walk a blockout and immediately understand intended encounters or navigation. As a practical habit, aim for quick iterations with one testable question per prototype. That keeps experiments focused and the feedback actionable. What single question will your next prototype answer? Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › What is Prototyping?
Definition

Prototyping is creating early, simplified versions of level spaces and mechanics to test specific gameplay questions quickly and cheaply.

Why it matters
  • Validates core mechanics before art investment.
  • Reveals scale and flow issues through direct play.
  • Enables faster team communication and alignment.
Key Takeaway

Treat prototypes as experiments with one clear question. If it fails, you learn. If it succeeds, you refine and add detail.

Concrete example
Example: Use cubes to lay out an arena, mark cover in red, elevated platforms in blue, then run a quick player run to test flank routes.
Analogy: A paper sketch for architecture — it shows circulation and proportions without finishes.
Common misconception: ‘‘I will wait for art to judge flow.’' Waiting increases cost of changes; test now with simple shapes.
Consider: what is the single player action you want to test in your next prototype?

screens.title: Blockout, Greybox, Whitebox — Stage Definitions
screens.subtitle: A clear process from rough layout to detailed block testing

narration.text: The prototyping process typically follows stages often labeled blockout, greybox, and whitebox. These names can be used interchangeably, but they emphasize a progression: start with very rough geometry to establish scale and flow, then refine collision and gameplay-critical shapes, and finally prepare a whitebox that closely mimics final gameplay without final art. In the earliest blockout you use large primitives to test walkable areas, while a greybox focuses on functional geometry—precise heights, ledge distances, and cover sizes. Whiteboxing pushes functional fidelity further, ensuring collisions and navigation mesh behavior are stable. A common misconception is that each stage requires long durations; instead, each stage should be as brief as necessary to answer a single question. Use short cycles: build, test, note, iterate. For instance, if your blockout shows a choke point causes slow pacing, you can widen the corridor or add an alternate route and re-test within minutes. This targeted loop keeps iteration cheap and focused on gameplay outcomes rather than visual polish. Which stage will you shorten to speed up your workflow? screens.title: Quick Blockout Workflow — Editor Steps
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step starter you can follow in Unity or Unreal

narration.text: Here is a concise, engine-agnostic workflow you can follow to produce a simple blockout. Start a new empty scene, add a large flat primitive for the floor and scale it to create the play area. Then add cubes for walls, pillars for cover, and larger cubes or stacked shapes for elevated platforms. Use the editor's manipulation tools—move, rotate, scale—and features like extrude or subtractive brushes to carve doorways and ramps. Apply simple unlit colors to indicate function: grey for floor, white for walls, red for cover, blue for elevated areas. Immediately test player movement: try every route an AI or player might take, check jumps, and verify whether sightlines allow intended encounters. Keep iterations small: change a single wall or cover piece, re-test, and log the result. A common misconception is that the workflow requires scripting or complex setup; for a blockout you only need primitives and the movement controller. The code-like starter below captures the essential steps you can run through in any editor. After you build the blockout, prepare a short playtest script that asks players a single open question to reveal clarity or confusion.

keyIdea.title: Practical steps
keyIdea.text: Follow a short, repeatable sequence: create floor, place primitives, color-code functions, test movement, iterate one change at a time.

Observation checklist: jump success rate, time spent in cover, preferred routes, camera collisions.
Pro Tip

screens.title: Conducting Effective Playtests
screens.subtitle: Design tests to reveal behavior, not confirm assumptions

narration.text: Playtesting is how you gather evidence about what players actually do in your level. Good playtests are short, focused, and observational. Start with a clear question—do players find the route, is the jump feasible, does cover lead to engaging combat? Use blind tests when you want to evaluate inherent clarity: give no instructions and let players explore. For controlled tests, give a specific objective but still observe deviations. Ask open-ended post-test questions like ‘‘What did you try first?’' or ‘‘How did you feel when you reached X?'' Avoid leading questions that bias answers. During the session, record behavior: where players hesitate, where they fail, and what they ignore. A common mistake is treating verbal feedback as final; always pair statements with observed actions. For example, a player might say they ‘‘liked the cover,'' but observation may show they never used it. Translate observations into specific iteration tasks: move a wall, add a route, or change platform spacing. End each session by prioritizing one high-impact change and one low-effort tweak to apply before the next test. Which small change will you prioritize after your next playtest?

keyIdea.title: Testing principle
keyIdea.text: Ask one clear question per test, observe actions first, and convert observations into a prioritized iteration plan.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Playtesting
Playtest recipe
  1. Define a single question to test.
  2. Choose blind or guided mode depending on clarity vs. objective testing.
  3. Observe behaviour: hesitation, repeated attempts, preferred routes.
  4. Ask open-ended follow-ups after observation.
  5. Prioritize one change and one quick tweak for the next iteration.
Observation cards
Hesitation point: where players stop and look around for cues.
Failure cluster: repeated attempts that indicate a mechanical or scale problem.
Ignored element: objects players never interact with, revealing poor affordance.
Common mistake
Ignoring observed behavior and leaning on what testers say. Always reconcile words with actions.

screens.title: Turning Playtest Notes into Iterations
screens.subtitle: How to prioritize changes and avoid feature creep

narration.text: Once you have playtest observations, the next step is to convert them into concrete iteration tasks. Start by separating issues into two axes: impact on gameplay and effort to implement. High-impact, low-effort fixes should be prioritized first. Examples include moving a cover piece that blocks a route or slightly widening a choke point. High-impact, high-effort items warrant discussion with artists or programmers before committing. Low-impact, low-effort tweaks can be batched. Avoid feature creep: each iteration should refine the prototype toward answering a measured question, not add new mechanics. A common misconception is that more features will fix unclear design. Often they mask the underlying problem. Instead, ask: which change will most directly test the observed behavior? Document a short rationale for every change so the next playtest measures that exact hypothesis. For instance, if players bypass a route because it's not visible, try a small geometry adjustment or a contrasting color to guide the eye, then re-test. Keep iterations short and measurable to preserve momentum. screens.title: Editor Tools: ProBuilder and BSP Brushes
screens.subtitle: How basic editor operations speed blockout creation

narration.text: Two common toolsets for rapid blockouts are ProBuilder in Unity and BSP brushes in Unreal. They both let you create and manipulate primitives in-editor so you can iterate geometry without external modeling. Typical operations you'll use include placing additive boxes for rooms, subtractive boxes to carve doorways, extruding faces to create platforms, and color-coding primitives to indicate function. The key affordance is speed: you should be able to create a candidate layout, test it, and adjust it in minutes. Don't assume complex operations are required; many blockouts are built from simple additions and subtractions. A common misconception is that these tools are only for artists — designers should own blockouts to test gameplay. Practice using basic commands: move, rotate, scale, extrude, and boolean add/subtract. When using subtractive brushes, confirm collision and navmesh behavior early, because these operations affect AI paths. Finally, label or color primitives consistently so teammates can interpret the blockout at a glance. Which editor operation will you practice until it's second nature? screens.title: What to Avoid During Prototyping
screens.subtitle: Common mistakes and how to prevent them

narration.text: Several predictable mistakes derail rapid prototyping. First, over-detailing too early: adding final art, complex props, or lighting before the layout is proven wastes time and makes later changes costly. Second, ignoring playtester behavior in favor of verbal feedback: what players do often contradicts what they say, so pair observations with notes. Third, not testing enough: a single internal pass is rarely sufficient. Fourth, designing in isolation: exclude artists, programmers, or QA and you risk integration problems later. Fifth, feature creep during iteration: adding new mechanics instead of refining existing ones expands scope and delays validation. To prevent these pitfalls, keep your prototypes functional, limit changes per iteration, ask one test question at a time, and invite at least one outside observer to playtest. Use a short checklist before you polish: can a player traverse intended routes, are jumps feasible, and do sightlines support planned encounters? Fix those first. screens.title: Activity: Blockout a Simple Combat Arena
screens.subtitle: Practical requirements and a starter template

narration.text: This activity asks you to create a simple blockout for a combat arena using only basic geometric shapes. The requirements are: a central open area for combat, at least three distinct cover points, at least two elevated positions with a way to reach them, and a clear entrance and exit. Use only cubes, planes, and cylinders with simple unlit colors to indicate function. Start by creating a flat floor scaled to about thirty units across. Place three low cover cubes around the center, and add two stacked cubes or a platform connected by a ramp for elevation. Apply contrasting colors so cover and elevated positions are obvious. Playtest the layout yourself: can the player move, jump, and use cover as intended? Observe and note one issue and perform one change to fix it. A common mistake is adding too many decorative objects; resist the urge and keep focus on tactical geometry. After the iteration, capture a screenshot from the player perspective and write a short note describing the tactical opportunities your arena offers. screens.title: Assessment Questions & Troubleshooting
screens.subtitle: How to diagnose common playtest failures

narration.text: This screen walks through two assessment-style scenarios and how to diagnose them. First scenario: players repeatedly get stuck at a puzzle point and try the same incorrect solution. The likely issue is unclear affordance or poor player guidance. The first iteration should be to re-evaluate the blockout: adjust geometry, make interactive objects visually distinct with color or contrast, or remove misleading elements. Avoid adding explicit hints prematurely. Second scenario: why greyboxing is beneficial compared to building with final art? The core benefit is speed and cheap modifications. Greyboxing reveals problems like impossible jumps or poor sightlines quickly, so you can adjust scale or spacing in minutes rather than reworking detailed assets. A common misconception is that greyboxes lack validity; in reality, functional clarity discovered in a greybox prevents expensive late-stage fixes. When troubleshooting, always log observed behavior, propose a single hypothesis, test that change, and measure results. This scientific approach keeps your iteration focused and verifiable. Do: change form or spacing. Don’t: immediately add UI hints or unrelated mechanics.

Greyboxing helps identify fundamental spatial or mechanical issues—impossible jumps, poor sightlines, or bad pacing—quickly and cheaply. Fixing these in a greybox avoids wasted artist time and costly rework later.

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact concept cards to carry forward

narration.text: Here are three essential concepts to remember and apply. First, prototyping: build simplified versions of a level to test scale, movement, and flow before committing art. Second, iteration: make one targeted change based on observed behavior, then re-test to confirm its effect. Third, blockout stages: progress from loose primitives to a whitebox with precise gameplay geometry, keeping fidelity aligned with the question you are testing. Internalize these as a loop: prototype to reveal issues, playtest to gather evidence, iterate to address them, and repeat. This loop reduces wasted work and focuses your team on what players actually do, not what designers imagine. Keep your prototypes inexpensive, your tests targeted, and your iterations measurable.
